source.title: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists - Doomsday Clock timeline

note: Official settings announced by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. Since 2007 the Clock has also weighed climate change, and more recently biosecurity and disruptive technologies, so it is not a nuclear-only measure.

settings.reason: The Clock's first setting, two years into the nuclear age.
The Soviet Union tests its first atomic device.
The United States and the Soviet Union test thermonuclear devices months apart.
Growing scientific cooperation and public awareness of shared risk.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty ends atmospheric testing by its signatories.
War in Vietnam and the Middle East; France and China build up arsenals.
The Non-Proliferation Treaty is ratified by nearly all nuclear powers.
SALT I and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty are signed.
Arms talks stall; India tests a nuclear device.
Deadlocked talks and rising nationalism.
Afghanistan, Poland and open superpower hostility.
The arms race accelerates and dialogue nearly stops.
The INF Treaty eliminates a whole class of missiles.
The Iron Curtain falls.
START is signed; the safest setting in the Clock's history.
Post-Soviet arsenals and materials are poorly secured.
India and Pakistan test nuclear weapons.
The US withdraws from the ABM Treaty; concern over unsecured material.
Climate change is added to the Clock's criteria alongside nuclear risk.
New START negotiations and the Copenhagen climate accord.
Inadequate action on nuclear weapons and on climate.
Unchecked climate change and arsenal modernisation.
Nuclear rhetoric escalates; the Clock moves in half-minutes for the first time.
Breakdown of the international order and of arms-control diplomacy.
The Clock switches to seconds: nuclear risk, climate and information warfare.
Russia's war in Ukraine and its nuclear signalling.
Nuclear risk, climate, biological threats and disruptive technologies.
The closest setting in the Clock's history.
